A man was killed in a single car crash around 7:17 am PST Monday, 1/31/2022. According to Washington State Patrol, speed and ice were factors in the collision which resulted when a man in a truck attempted to speed past another vehicle, then lost control after hitting a patch of ice while on an overpass on Highway 303. The truck struck and rolled over a Jersey barrier, falling onto the road below. The driver died in the|crash, while a passenger sustained only minor injuries. Temperatures around the area were generally in the 30 to 33 degree range at the time of the incident and according to a media report icy roads ...were reported around the region with similar reports from Central Kitsap Fire and Rescue.

Heavy rainfall of 6 to 10 inches, along with melting of remaining snow at lower elevations, lead to river flooding, significant urban and small stream flooding, and landslides. The peak of the rainfall was January 5 through January 7. Major flooding occurred on the Chehalis River and moderate flooding on the Satsop River. A motorist was stranded trying to cross a flooded road along the Chehalis River and was swept away when he left his vehicle. He was missing and presumed dead. Another man fatality occurred when an man tried to move his car out of flood danger and the car was swept away by flooding on the North River. Damages are reported and estimated; not all damages have been identified. Crop damages are unknown.

On a warm and dry 22nd of March, 2014, a large landslide occurred four miles east of the town of Oso, Washington. The slide debris, traveling at over 60 miles per hour, crossed the entire river valley, covering an area of over a square mile with an approximate deposit thickness of 15 to 75 feet in some areas. The force of the slide flow caused 43 fatalities, 12 injuries, destroyed 37 homes, and wiped out SR 530 for over a mile. In addition, the slide debris completely blocked the North Fork Stillaguamish River for over 24 hours, backing up a pool of water that flooded the valley about 2 miles upstream and reached approximately 20 feet deep, inundating an additional 6 homes. The cause of the slide is not fully known, though precipitation in the previous months to years contributed to the ground failure. A rain gage located 2 miles west of the slide had 19.93 inches of rain in the 40 days leading up to the slide. |As of March 19th the nearest reporting station Arlington, had reported 7.14 inches of rain, which is about 2 inches shy of the record 9.23 for the entire month of March.  Three days before the slide, the area received close to an inch of rain in one day. Most all of the fatalities occurred at the permanent homes impacted by the slide.

On 10/04/2019 a brief weak tornado was confirmed by video and fire/rescue report near Tenino, WA. No impacts or damage were observed.

Between approximately 6:02 - 6:07 PM on the evening of October 18, a tornado touched down near Shelton in Mason County, Washington and traveled approximately 0.68 miles before moving over the water of Pickering Passage and dissipating as a waterspout. The first video evidence and reports from area fire officials prompted the NWS to send a damage survey team to the area during the afternoon of October 19, 2019. Preliminary evaluation of the damage by the team concluded that the tornado reached an EF-1 rating. The damage path was up to 90 yards in width and the tornado was estimated to be on the ground for approximately 5 minutes.||Fortunately, no injuries were reported with this tornado. Most of the damage was in the form of uprooted or snapped soft wood fir and cedar trees. Falling trees did impact at least two houses along the damage path, including one house that had two trees fall on the roof.

A Quinault Indian Nation Fire official reported that at approximately 5:20 AM he came upon 10 downed trees (1-2.5 feet in diameter) across Moclips Highway (S-26) at approximately mile marker 18. Photographs were provided of the downed trees. Subsequent reports and imagery from a trained spotter identified additional damage approximately 0.5 miles to the northeast across a forest service road. No injuries or other impacts were reported.||An evaluation of the photographic evidence from local officials and the trained spotter combined with radar signatures from the event are consistent with a brief tornado. Based on the location and path length the tornado most likely touched down at 4:40am and lasted for less than 2 minutes, traveling 0.50 miles with a maximum width of 30 yards. The degree of tree damage is consistent with peak winds of approximately 90 MPH, rating it as an EF-1 tornado on the Enhanced Fujita scale.

Anomalous upper level high pressure combined with surface low pressure near the WA Coast and high pressure east of the WA Cascades led to the favorable set up for wildfires across the area. With the development of strong Cascade gap winds from the east, the Sumner Grade fire was ignited as strong winds downed trees onto power lines. The fire burned 800 acres before becoming contained. The fire causes structural damage, school closings, power outages, and evacuations.

Anomalous upper level high pressure over the Northwest US in combination with surface low pressure along the WA Coast and high pressure east of the WA Cascades led to the development of favorable wildfire conditions. This particular set up led to the development of strong east winds through the Cascades gaps amidst dry antecedent conditions. In Graham, WA several brushfires were initially reported as windy conditions knocked over power lines. These brushfires later combined to form a larger wildfire that led to evacuations of local residents, and eventually structural damage to local homes and buildings. The fire burned 275 acres before becoming contained on Sept 13.

Strong easterly winds through the Cascade gaps led to the development of a wildfire around Enumclaw on September 8. The wildfire burned 132 acres and caused the closure of SR 410 for several weeks from Enumclaw to Greenwater WA as crews had to remove trees to continue firefighting operations. After the containment, crews had to conduct rock scaling and begin guardrail repair.

During a period of strong easterly winds, three vessels moored on the outside breakwater at Seabeck marina in Hood Canal. The wind and wave action caused them to impact the dock. The damage included severe denting of hull and upper deck, one of the vessels was holed and took on water,  and one vessel has its engines moved about 3/4 in causing misalignment of prop shafts. All vessels had damage to the Starboard side.

The ignition of multiple wildfires across the Pacific Northwest around Labor Day led to a period of poor air quality by mid-September as dense smoke combined with low level moisture and fog. Alaska Airlines suspended all flights to and from airports in Seattle and Portland, a Seattle Mariners game vs the San Fransisco Giants was postponed due to poor air quality, and all city of Seattle beaches, boat ramps, parks, and play fields closed amidst poor air quality around Sept 15. Many COVID19 sites also closed due to poor air quality. Dense smoke, haze, and poor air quality remained a problem for days across all of Washington.

Strong easterly winds resulted in an estimated 2500 customers without power by the early morning hours of September 8. During the afternoon of the 7th, tree limbs fell on power lines in the Fife and Browns Point areas, with around 5000 customers losing power.|| Several brush fires were reported during this period of strong winds: a brush fire closed SR 512 at I-5, a brush fire closed S 56th St, a brush fire closed the I-5 offramp to Martin Way in Olympia, a brush fire blocked several lanes of I-5 near Federal Way.

Strong easterly winds resulted in widespread power outages in the Seattle metro area as tree limbs fell onto power lines. The town of Burien reported tree branches falling on wires, resulting in a power outage affecting 5300 customers. Seattle City Light reported a power outage near Beacon Hill affecting 5000 customers.||Several brush fires were also reported during this period of strong wind.

Large waves in tandem with King Tides led to coastal flooding along the Central Coast of Washington on Nov 15. Numerous reports and pictures/videos were posted on Twitter, with flooding noticeable in parking lots and within business districts. Westport appeared to be hardest hit, with several businesses experiencing flooding in the Marina District. Hazardous ocean conditions led to copious amounts of gravel to build up over Half Moon Bay. This helped seawater flow directly into the business district as well as inundate Westhaven Drive.

Around 9pm on Nov 17, a rogue wave caused a Tulalip Police Department Fisheries vessel that was assisting another vessel to capsize near Jetty Island. Search and rescue efforts were hampered by stormy weather and heavy seas with debris. One person was rescued shortly before midnight, with another person initially listed as missing. Recovery efforts continued, with the missing person never found and presumed to be dead.

Reports of a quick 1-4 inches of new snow (an isolated report of 6 inches) was reported between Port Angeles and Sequim. Washington State Patrol responded to multiple vehicle spinouts and a car accident on US 101 between Lake Crescent (MP 231) and Hansen Road (MP 240).

A strong cold frontal passage brought a changeover from rain to wet, dense snow during the afternoon hours on December 21. These conditions led to a quick accumulation of generally 1-2 inches of snow (with an isolated report of 5 inches)  that covered grassy surfaces and some roadways, leading to hazardous travel conditions.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF WHATCOM AND SKAGIT COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Heavy snow in the North Cascades led to new accumulations of around 20 inches in 24 hours.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF SNOHOMISH AND KING COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Heavy snow in the Central Cascades beginning the evening of the 29th led to a new 24 hour snow accumulation at Snoqualmie Pass of almost 20 inches by the evening of the 30th. Heavy snow would then continue into the morning hours of the 31st. Stevens Pass received less snowfall. On December 30, I-90 eastbound at North Bend (MP 34) was closed due to spinouts around 1PM.

Fort Ebey State Park was forced to close for a period of time on December 30 due to numerous downed trees, per WA State Parks. The ferry service from 8am-1030am from Port Townsend and Coupeville were cancelled due to high wind and rough seas.
During the morning hours of January 2, Mesonet EW2796 reported a wind gust of 58 mph 9 miles northwest of Langley.

Around 10 AM, the Mesonet XMPL 4 miles E/SE of Port Townsend at the Marrowstone Pt Lighthouse in Jefferson County reported a wind gust of 59 mph. Mesonet FW4667 also reported a wind gust of 59 mph around 1030 AM.

During the late morning hours, Mesonet CW3375 near Ferndale, Washington reported a wind gust of 62 mph. Nearby Mesonet CW1394 6 miles west of Marietta near Sandy Pt Shores reported a wind gust of 61 mph.
During the late morning hours, KNUW at the Naval Air Station on Whidbey Island reported a wind gust of 58 mph.

Wind forecast for the Admiralty Inlet area led to the cancellation of all ferry sailing to Port Townsend and Coupeville during the morning hours of the 5th. Mesonet stations in Jefferson and Island counties reported wind gusts between 52-57 mph from mid-morning through early afternoon.

During the morning and early afternoon hours, strong winds plagued the San Juan Islands, with Mesonet DW7371 reporting a wind gust of 60 mph on Lopez Island. Mesonet DW5375 on Decatur Island reported a wind gust of 59 mph. Trees on power lines also caused power outages on Orcas Island.

A wind gust of 58 mph was reported near Toms Creek in Clallam County shortly after 3am. Winds began to pick up across Clallam County during the late evening hours on the 12th and continued into the early morning hours of the 13th. Other wind gust reports around the county ranged from 40 mph to 55 mph. Owl Mountain reported a wind gust of 58 mph.

Wind gusts of around 60 mph were reported across Grays Harbor County beginning during the late evening hours of the 12th and continuing through the early morning hours of the 13th. Humptullips reported a gust of 62 mph, with the Hoquiam airport reporting a gust of 58 mph and Ocean shores at 59 mph.

The Naval Air Station on Whidbey Island reported a wind gust of 64 mph shortly after midnight on January 13. Other locations in the vicinity, including Camano Island and Camano City reported gusts of 58 mph and 44 mph, respectively. ||A semi truck on SR 20 driving over the Deception Pass Bridge lost control in high winds and was partially hanging over the edge of the bridge, blocking all traffic over the bridge for several hours.

Areas around the Seattle metro reported wind gusts ranging from 40-60 mph beginning during the late evening hours and through the early morning hours of the 13th. SeaTac reported a wind gust of 58 mph, with Federal Way reporting 61 mph, both shortly after midnight. The Seattle Tacoma Airport reported a wind gust of 49 mph, with other locations reporting wind gusts of 52 mph (Bellevue), 46 mph (Renton Airport), 54 mph (Des Moines).||Multiple roads in Seattle were closed due to downed powerlines during the early morning hours.

Areas around Tacoma reported wind gusts of 40-60 mph beginning during the late evening hours on the 12th and continuing through the early morning hours of the 13th. Ft Lewis and JBLM reported gusts of 58 mph, with other reports of 56 mph (Tacoma), 58 mph (Greenwater).||In South Tacoma, a tree came down on a home and demolished it, trapping one of the occupants (occupant was rescued and unharmed).||The North Meridian Bridge closed in both directions for a period of time due to a tree hitting the bridge and causing damage to the bridge.

Strong winds affected Western Whatcom County, beginning during the late evening hours of the 12th and continuing through the early morning hours of the 13th. Sandy Pt Shores reported a wind gust of 72 mph and Ferndale reported a gust of 70 mph. Other reports included: 65 mph (Birch Bay), 52 mph (Lynden), 49 mph (Bellingham), 45 mph (Chuckanut Village).
Coastal flooding inundated a picnic area at Rialto Beach in Olympic National Park during the morning hours of January 13.
Coastal Flooding from King Tides led to flooding of the Bridge Community Center in Birch Bay.

The Grays Harbor County Sheriff's Office reported a fatality near the Pacific Beach State Park around 10:30 AM on January 10. A 54 year old woman from Oak Harbor, Washington was killed after being struck by a log on the beach. She and her husband were walking on the beach when a large set of waves came in and they stood on top of the log to avoid the waves. A wave knocked both of them of the log and rolled over them.

events.cz_name: EASTERN STRAIT OF JUAN DE FUCA
events.event_narrative: After strong winds affected the area beginning during the late evening hours of 12th and through the early morning hours of the 13th, the USCG reported and responded to multiple vessels impacted by high winds around Anacortes, Washington. A pier sunk, and several boats were pulled loose from moorings, with one floating adrift.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF SNOHOMISH AND KING COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Winter weather affected the Central Cascades at the beginning of the New Year. About 15 inches of new snow fell at Snoqualmie Pass beginning around noon on January 2nd through the evening hours on January 3. During the evening hours of January 2, I-90 EB was closed at MP 46 due to a spun out semi truck. Stevens Pass also experienced heavy snow during this event, with around 18-19 inches of snow within a 24 hour period extending from roughly 1PM January 2 through 1PM January 3. This prompted US 2 to close in both directions between MP 72 and MP 80 given hazardous road conditions.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF WHATCOM AND SKAGIT COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Heavy snow began to fall in the North Cascades during the early morning hours of January 2 and continued to fall before tapering around sunrise on January 3. NWAC snowfall observations indicate new snowfall amounts of around 20-25 inches near the Mount Baker Ski Area within this event.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF PIERCE AND LEWIS COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Heavy snow began to fall in the Southern Cascades during the early afternoon hours on January 2. By 12 PM on January 3 (24 hours later), 21-22 inches of new snow were reported around Paradise at Mount Rainier National Park. Snow then gradually tapering into the evening hours.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF WHATCOM AND SKAGIT COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Light snow began falling during the early morning hours of January 5, increasing in intensity through the evening and overnight hours of the 6th. In a 24 hour period, NWAC snowfall data indicated a little over 20 inches of new snow near the Mount Baker Ski Resort. Snow then quickly tapered through the rest of the morning on the 6th.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF PIERCE AND LEWIS COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Light snow began during the morning hours of the 5th, peaking in intensity during the evening of the 5th and overnight into the 6th. According to NWAC snow data, from arounf 6PM PST on the 5th through 6AM PST on the 6th, around 12 inches of new fell around Paradise at Mount Rainier National Park. Light snow then continued through the remainder of the morning before tapering.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF WHATCOM AND SKAGIT COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Snow began during the evening hours of January 11th and quickly increased in coverage overnight and through the morning hours of the 12th. Heavy snow then continued through the night of the 12th into the early morning hours of the 13th. According to NWAC snow data, from around 6AM PST on the 12th through 6AM PST on the 13th, around 22 inches of new snow fell around the Mount Baker Ski Resort.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF SNOHOMISH AND KING COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Snow began falling during the morning hours on the 11th and continued through the 12th. In a 12 hour period, spanning from roughly 5PM PST on the 11th through 5AM PST on the 12th, around 14 inches of new snow was recorded at Snoqualmie Pass. Overall, throughout the entirety of this event from around 11 AM PST on the 11th through 6AM on the 12th around 19 inches of new snow fell around Snoqualmie Pass.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF WHATCOM AND SKAGIT COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Snow began just after midnight on the 30th and continued through the 31st. 24 hour snow amounts beginning around 6AM PST on the 30th through 6AM PST on the 31st around the Mount Baker Ski Resort were around 20 inches.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF SNOHOMISH AND KING COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Light snow began to fall around Stevens Pass and the nearby Central Cascades around day break on February 4th and began to pick up in intensity around 6PM. From the evening hours of February 4th to daybreak on February 5th ( a 12 hour period), around 14 inches of new snow fell. Snow then tapered through the remaining hours of the morning on the 5th.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF SNOHOMISH AND KING COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Snow began falling around daybreak on February 6th and continued through the morning hours on February 7th, heavy at times. In a 24 hour period spanning roughly from 8am on February 6th to 8am on February 7th, around 19 inches of new snow fell at Stevens Pass.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF PIERCE AND LEWIS COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Snow began near daybreak on February 6th and continued through the early morning hours of February 8th. Snow was heaviest on the 6th, from around sunrise through midnight. In a 12 hour period from roughly 8am to 8pm on February 6th, Paradise at Mount Rainier picked up around 14 inches of new snow.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF SNOHOMISH AND KING COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: A prolonged period of snowfall occurred across the Cascades in the middle of February. Snow began falling on February 14th, increasing in intensity on February 15th. Then, between the hours of 6am on February 16th and 6am on February 17th snowfall peaked in intensity around Stevens Pass, with 20 inches of new reported during this time period. Snoqualmie Pass also experienced heavy snow during this prolonged event. Snowfall at Snoqualmie Pass peaked in intensity on the 15th, with 11 inches of new snow reported between 6am to 6pm on the 15th.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF SNOHOMISH AND KING COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Snow began in the Central Cascades on February 21st and peaked in intensity on February 22nd. In a 12 hour period spanning from 6am to 6pm on February 22nd, around 15 inches of new snow fell across Stevens Pass. Snow then tapered into the night, with a few more inches reported by sunrise on the 23rd. In total, around 19 inches of new snow fell in a 24 hour period spanning from 6am on the 22nd to 6am on the 23rd.||In addition to heavy snowfall, the presence of high avalanche danger amidst an unstable snowpack caused WSDOT to to close all major cross-cascade highways, including US 2 over Stevens Pass and I-90 over Snoqualmie Pass the evening of February 21st through the morning of February 22nd. After opening the morning of the 22nd, additional snowfall then led WSDOT to re-close US 2 over Stevens Pass. Avalanches were reported near the Pass after the highway closed, along with reports of snow slides blocking the road on the east side of the Pass between MP 58 and 85. The highway did not reopen until February 23rd.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF SNOHOMISH AND KING COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Snow noticeably began to pick up across the Central Cascades shortly after midnight on February 25th and continued through daybreak on the 26th. During a 24 hour period from roughly 7am on the 25th to 7am on the 26th, Stevens Pass reported around 20 inches if new snow.

High winds were reported around Sandy Point Shores on February 11 in strong Fraser outflow out of the northeast. Gusts were reported by observation sites C1394 and KWAFERND4 of 71 and 72 mph, respectively. These gusty winds also made for cold morning wind chills.

During the overnight hours on February 12th, reports from the public began to come in regarding significant (at least 1/4) ice accumulation on many surfaces. Areas from around Ocean Shores to Pacific reportedly received the highest amounts of ice accumulation. Precipitation would then move more inland/to the east during the later morning hours, ending the highest chances for ice.

Snow began to spread across Western Whatcom County during the late overnight period of February 12 into February 13th. Local CocoRaHs observations by daybreak on the 13th showed generally 3-5 inches of new snow across the western portion of the county. Snow would then taper through the afternoon, with generally minimal additional accumulation.

A significant winter storm brought heavy snowfall to the San Juan Islands late in the evening and into the overnight period from February 12 to February 13. Local CoCoRaHs reports around daybreak on February 13 ranged from generally 5-10 inches of snow through that short time period.

A significant winter storm impacted Western Skagit County late in the evening hours on February 12 and continued through the overnight and morning period of February 13. Some areas within the County recorded around 8-9 inches of new snow in a 12 hour period.

A significant winter storm impacted the Admiralty Inlet area beginning during the late evening hours of February 12 and into the morning hours of February 13. Most locations received less than 4 inches in a 12 hour period (generally 1-3 inches area-wide), however, a few locations on Camano Island received 4 inches, mainly on the northern side of the island.

A major winter storm impacted the Bellevue area beginning during the late evening hours of February 12 and continuing through the morning hours of February 13. Within a 12 hours period, many CoCoRaHs reports ranged from 5-9 inches. Snow then slowly tapered through the afternoon and evening hours with little additional accumulation.

A major winter storm impacted the Bremerton area beginning during the late evening hours on February 12 and continuing through the morning hours of February 13. Within a 12 hour window, many local CoCoRaHs stations reported new snowfall totals in the 6-10 inch range. Light snow would continue through the afternoon and gradually taper into the evening, with little additional accumulation.

A major winter storm impacted the Everett area/western Snohomish County during the late evening hours of February 12 through the morning hours of February 13. In roughly a 12 hour window, many local CoCoRaHs stations reported new snow accumulations of between 4-7 inches. Snow continued through into the afternoon hours and gradually tapered, with little additional accumulation.

A significant winter storm impacted the Hood Canal area beginning during the evening hours of February 12 and continuing through the morning hours of February 13. Local CoCoRaHs observations around sunrise on February 13 suggested new snowfall totals ranging from 4-12 inches along the Canal vicinity. Snow would continue into the afternoon while gradually tapering. Little additional snow accumulation was reported.

Significant snowfall impacted the Lower Chehalis Valley beginning during the late afternoon and early evening hours of February 12 and continuing through the overnight period into February 13. Snowfall amounts during this general timeframe ranged from between 5-9 inches. Snow gradually tapered into the afternoon hours on February 13, with little additional snowfall accumulation thereafter.

A major winter storm impacted the Seattle area beginning during the late evening hours on February 12 and continuing through the morning hours on February 13. Local CoCoRaHs observations indicated new snowfall totals in the 4-10 inch range. Snow continued through the afternoon hours while gradually tapering. Little additional snowfall accumulation was reported.

After receiving several inches of light snow on February 11, a much more significant winter storm affected the Southwest Interior, beginning during the late afternoon and early evening hours on February 12 and continuing through the morning hours of February 13. Local CoCoRaHs observations indicated new snowfall totals from the 12th into the 13th of generally 8-11 inches.

A major winter storm affected the Tacoma area beginning during the evening hours of February 12 and continuing through the morning hours of February 13. Local CoCoRaHs observations indicated new snowfall amounts of between 6-8 inches. Snow continued through the morning hours before gradually tapering. Little additional snowfall was reported.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF WHATCOM AND SKAGIT COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Snow began to fall in the North Cascades around noon on March 28. Within a 12 hour period, 24 inches of new snow was recorded at the Mount Baker Ski Area. Snow then continued through the early morning hours on the 29th before ending.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF SNOHOMISH AND KING COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Snow began around midday on the 28th across the Central Cascades and within 12 hours, 13 inches of new snow was recorded at Stevens Pass. Snow then continued through the morning hours of the 29th before coming to an end.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF WHATCOM AND SKAGIT COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Snow began to fall in the North Cascades during the mid-morning hours of April 7th. Snow accumulated quickly as snow levels dropped to 2000 feet or below. The Mount Baker Ski area recorded around 13.5 inches of new snow in a 12 hour period between 9am and 9pm. Snow continued into the overnight period, gradually tapering into the morning hours of the 8th.
A section of pavement came loose/buckled on NB I-405 and I-5 in Tukwila, causing road and highway closures for several hours during the evening commute.

State route 544 milepost 7 near Everson was closed as asphalt roadway buckled and was deemed unsafe for travel. Detours were put in place with highway repair complete the morning following the incident.

Concrete panels along NB I-5 to I-705 experienced period damage and needed continuous repairs from Jun 27-Jun 29. This caused 3 lanes of the collector-distributor to close, causing traffic backups and detours.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF SNOHOMISH AND KING COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: The left two lanes of I-90 eastbound five miles east of North Bend closed due to the highway buckling from the heat. This lead to traffic and difficult travel conditions.

Record breaking heat across the Seattle metro area led to multiple heat related fatalities, numerous pavement buckles requiring road closures and repair, the closing of University bridge for marine traffic due to excessive heat, lowering of speed limits to Sound Transit, millions of gallons of water used, the highest energy usage in Seattle public utilities history during the summer months, the closing of the Seattle monorail, and the death of dozens of Caspian Terns.||Temperatures began to rise in the Seattle metro on 6/26 to 102 degrees, followed by an increase in several degrees to 104 on 6/27, with a peak and all time record high temperature on 6/28  of 108. Temperatures slowly began to cool as the month concluded.

Record breaking heat led to multiple days of high temperatures above 100 degrees. On 6/26 high temperatures rose to 102 degrees, with 6/27 several degrees warmer at 105. On 6/28 an all time record high temperature was set at the Olympia Airport of 110 degrees. Temperatures then began to cool during the final two days of June.||Centralia also unofficially tied its all time record high temperature of 107 degrees on 6/28.

Record breaking heat affected the Tacoma area for several days, beginning on 6/26 and peaking 6/27-6/28.  A high temperature of 99 was recorded on 6/27, with an (unofficial) all time record high temperature of 105 of 6/27. Temperatures then reached 99 and 97 on the afternoon of 6/28 and 6/29, respectively before a gradual cool down began at the conclusion of the month. Several reports of road buckling/road damage around Tacoma.

Record breaking heat from 6/26-6/29. High temperatures at the Bremerton airport reached 90 degrees on 6/26, followed by a noticeable warmup on 6/27 at 100 degrees. An (unofficial) all time record high temperature was reported on 6/28 at 102 degrees. The heat stuck around for one more day on 6/29 where high temperatures reached 101 in the afternoon before a gradual cool down commenced at the conclusion of the month.

An extended period of hot temperatures affected the Everett area from 6/26-6/28. Temperatures reached the mid 90s on the afternoons of both 6/26 and 6/27, with temperatures then peaking on 6/28 over 100 degrees. The Everett-Paine Airport unofficially tied its all time record high temperature of 100, with a nearby COOP site reporting 101 degrees. Several heat related illness incidents were reported during this time frame as well as a brushfire on I-5 NB near MP 197. Temperatures then cooled down back into the low 80s at the conclusion of the month, ending the record breaking heat.

events.cz_name: EASTERN STRAIT OF JUAN DE FUCA
events.event_narrative: Record breaking heat affected the Port Angeles area and nearby land locations around the Eastern Strait of Juan de Fuca. The Port Angeles airport recorded an (unofficial) all time record high temperature of 99 degrees on 6/28. Temperatures from 6/26-6/27 were in the mid 90s, with temperatures dropping back into the 70s by 6/29, ended the heat wave.

An extended period of hot temperatures affected western Whatcom County at the end of June. High temperatures reached the mid 90s on the afternoons of 6/26 and 6/27 according to the Bellingham Airport ASOS. Temperatures then peaked on 6/28 with a high temperature of 99 at the Bellingham Airport. This then became an all time record high temperature. By 6/29, temperatures cooled back into the upper 70s, ending the extended period of record breaking hot weather. In addition to the heat, there were some reports of road buckling on SR 544 near MP 7 near Everson.

Record breaking heat affected the North Coast of Washington at the end of June as a strong area of high pressure built into the region. The hottest afternoon temperatures were reported on the afternoon of 6/28, with the Quillayute Airport reporting an all time record high temperature of 110 degrees. The following day, onshore flow led to rapid cooling back into the upper 60s.

Recorded breaking heat affected the central Coast of Washington at the end of June as a strong area of high pressure became centered over the region. Temperatures began to increase into the upper 80s on 6/26, with temperatures peaking on 6/27 and remaining hot through 6/28. The Hoquiam airport recorded an all time record high temperature  on 6/27 of 103 degrees. At the conclusion of the month, temperatures began to cool back into the upper 60s as onshore flow strengthened and high pressure weakened.||Aberdeen also recorded an unofficial all time record high temperature on 6/28 of 108 degrees.

An extended period of hot weather affected the San Juan Islands at the end of June. The ASOS at Friday Harbor recorded high temperatures in the mid 90s from 6/26-6/28 before temperatures finally began to cool on 6/29.

An extended period of hot temperatures affected Western Skagit county at the end of June. The official COOP site was not active during the heat wave, but observations at KAWO reported a high temperature of 103 on 6/28. Temperatures peaked on 6/28, with hot conditions present from 6/26-6/27. Temperatures began to cool on 6/29 through the rest of the month.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF PIERCE AND LEWIS COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: An extended period of heat affected the Cascades of Pierce and Lewis Counties at the end of June. Temperatures began to climb  into the upper 70s and lower 80s at Paradise on 6/26 and continued through 6/28. On 6/29, the Paradise Ranger Station recorded an unofficial all time record high temperature of 90. Temperatures then remained above normal through the end of the month but were not as hot as the previous several days.||Longmire also unofficially tied its all time record high temperature on both 6/29 and 6/30 at 105 degrees.||Due to the extended period of extreme heat, flooding from glacial/snow melt washed out the Nisqually bridge near Cougar Rock. This affected hiking near Mount Rainier National Park.

A period of much above normal temperatures affected the Seattle area around mid-August. High temperatures ranged from the mid 80s to low 90s during this period, with the temperature peaking August 12-August 13 at 93 degrees, both of which were record high temperatures. Low temperatures during this period ranged from the mid to upper 60s.

The Southwest Interior experienced a stretch of heat towards mid August. The ASOS sensor at Olympia showed high temperatures in the low to mid 90s through the duration of the heat event, with a record high temperatures of 96 recorded on August 12. Low temperatures through the event ranged from the mid to upper 50s.||Centralia also recorded temperatures in the low to mid 90s. A high temperature of 95 was recorded on August 12 and August 13. Low temperatures stayed in the mid 60s.

A warm stretch of weather affected Western Whatcom County towards the middle of August, high temperatures consistently reached the mid to upper 80s for much of the duration of the heat stretch, however, temperatures soared to 100 degrees at the Bellingham Airport on August 12, setting a new record. Low temperatures during the event remained right around 60.

Very warm weather affected the Bremerton Area and the Kitsap Peninsula around the middle of August. Observations from Bremerton Fire showed high temperatures ranging from the mid 80s to low 90s through the duration of the event. Temperatures peaked on August 13, where a record high temperature of 93 was set. Low temperatures ranged from the low to mid 60s.

A warm stretch of weather affected the Everett area towards mid August. Temperatures ranged from the upper 80s to low 90s during the event, with a record high temperature of 92 degrees. Low temperatures ranged from the mid to upper 60s.||Everett-Paine Field airport had temperatures range from the upper 80s to low 90s, with a record high temperature set on August 13 of 91.

Warm weather affected the Tacoma area around mid August. Temperatures ranged in the upper 80s through the duration of the event, with the highest temperature recorded on August 12 at 89 degrees. This set a new record high temperature for that day. Low temperatures ranged from the mid to upper 60s.

A stretch of unusually warm weather affected the Lower Chehalis valley in mid August. Temperatures ranged from the upper 90s to low 100s during the event. A record high temperature of 101 was set on both August 12 and August 13, per a source sited from Elma, WA. Low temperatures ranged from the mid to upper 50s.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF WHATCOM AND SKAGIT COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Warm weather affected The Cascades valleys during mid August. Temperatures observed at Darrington ranged from the upper 80s to mid 90s, with lows in the upper 50s to near 60. Concrete observed temperatures in the mid 80s to low 90s, with a record high of 93 on August 13. Low temperatures ranged from the upper 50s to mid 60s.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF SNOHOMISH AND KING COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: A stretch of warm weather affected the valleys and lower elevations of the Central Cascades of King and Snohomish Counties. Monroe recorded temperatures in the upper 80s to low 90s during the event, with a record high of 91 on August 13 and August 14. Low temperatures ranged from the mid 50s to around 60.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF PIERCE AND LEWIS COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: A stretch of unusually warm weather affected the valleys and lower elevations of the Cascades of Lewis and Pierce Counties. Temperature recordings at Longmire at Mount Rainier National Park showed temperatures ranging from the mid 80s to upper 90s through the event, with record high temperatures of 98 degrees set on August 13 and August 14. Low temperatures ranged from the mid to upper 50s.||Cedar Lake also recorded temperatures in the mid to upper 80s, with a record high of 87 on August 14.

Puget Sound energy data revealed most of Whidbey Island without power due to strong gusty winds during the evening hours of Friday 9/17. A wind advisory had been upgraded to a High Wind Warning to account for this. Winds then gradually subsided through late evening. ||-One observation on Whidbey Island reported a sustained wind of 47 knots with gusts to 63 knots around 6pm on 9/17.||-WSDOT ferry route from Port Townsend/Coupeville service had been suspended due to high winds and rough seas.
During the morning hours of 9/18, WSDOT reported trees blocking all lanes on SR 9 NB and SB just north of SR 534 (MP 40). Trees were cleared by late morning, with wind speeds easing.

events.cz_name: EASTERN STRAIT OF JUAN DE FUCA
events.event_narrative: Strong winds affected the Eastern Strait of Juan de Fuca for much of the day on Friday 9/17. Downed trees were reported across much of Jefferson County, eventually prompting an upgrade from a Wind Advisory to a High Warning Warning. The following reports were gathered:||-Tree limbs were reported to be downed onto wires at Hastings and Howard in Port Townsend.||-The WSDOT ferry route from Port Townsend/Coupeville service was suspended due to strong winds and rough seas.||-A low hanging power line had US 101 at MP 276 near Old Gardiner Road reduced to one lane with alternating traffic. Old Gardiner Road was also blocked.||-Trees down on US 101 both directions at MP 167.59 near Lower Hoh Rd beginning at 1:16 pm on Sept. 17. Traffic was alternated through the area, with the area cleared an hour later.

The ASOS at Friday Harbor in the San Juan Islands reported a gust of 54 mph around 2245L on 10/24.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF SNOHOMISH AND KING COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Eastside Fire & Rescue says two people died when a tree fell on their car in the 7700 block of Preston Fall City Rd SE. As wind blew and rain fell, a huge tree snapped, then plunged onto the roadway at about 3 p.m. on Preston-Fall City Road.Camille Martlin, 59, and her son Max Martlin, 22 were instantly killed when the tree hit their car.|Fresh pumpkins were in the trunk.

Heavy rain and some snow melt caused flooding that exceeded major severity on the South Fork Nooksack River and mainstem Nooksack River at North Cedarville and Ferndale. There was urban and small stream flooding as well, hitting Bellingham especially hard. The heavy rain also triggered a dozen landslides throughout the area. Significant flooding on the Nooksack River also overflowed at the City of Everson to the degree that flood waters flowed north along an old Nooksack floodway and Johnson Creek where it flooded the cities of Everson and Nooksack, WA, then combined with flooding from the Sumas River and flooded the City of Sumas, WA where over 85% of homes sustained water damage. Damages are reported and estimated; not all damages have been identified. Crop damages are unknown.

Heavy rain and some snow melt caused flooding throughout much of Skagit County, especially on the Skagit and Samish Rivers. Flooding on the Skagit started on the 12th, then temporarily dropped below flood stage, before rising to major flood on the night of the 14th. 2 fatalities occurred during this time with many road, highways, and bridges  closed due to water over roadway, washouts, sloughing, and debris. Town inundated including Rockport, Hamilton, Lyman, Sedro Woolley, and Mount Vernon.  There was urban and small stream flooding as well on the 15th.The heavy rain also triggered a number of landslides throughout the area. Damages are reported and estimated; not all damages have been identified. Crop damages are unknown.

Heavy rain and some snow melt caused flooding throughout much of Clallam County, especially on the Bogachiel and Elwha Rivers. Flooding reached major severity and preliminarily a record stage. Many road, highways, and bridges  closed due to water over roadway, washouts, sloughing, and debris. There was urban and small stream flooding as well on the 14th - 15th. The heavy rain also triggered a number of landslides throughout the area. Damages are reported and estimated; not all damages have been identified. Crop damages are unknown.
Flooding of minor category occurred on the Skagit and Samish Rivers, as well as other streams and urban areas.

The Skokomish River went above flood stage December 31st, 2020 and stayed above flood stage until January 7, closing roads and cutting off access to the valley. I was above moderate flood at times everyday from January 2nd and the 6th. Urban and small stream flooding occurred as well.

The Satsop River hit flood stage on the 2nd and Moderate flood stage on the 3rd. Flooding on the Chehalis River at Porter started on the 5th, cresting above Moderate flood before falling below flood on the 11th. Urban and small stream flooding occurred as well.
The Skookumchuck River near Bucoda and Chehalis River near Grand Mound exceeded moderate flood stage. Urban and small stream flooding occurred as well.
The Chehalis River near Doty, Newaukum River near Centralia rose above flood stage Jan 3.  Urban and small stream flooding occurred as well.
The Bogachiel River was above flood stage Jan 3 to 4, 2021.
Heavy rain drove a several rivers and streams above flood stage. Major flooding occurred on the Cowlitz River and moderate flooding on the Newaukum River.

Heavy rain and snow melt pushed a number of rivers above flood stage. Moderate flooding occurred on the Snohomish and Skykomish Rivers, with minor flooding on the Stillaguamish. Several pulses of heavy rain from the 3 atmospheric rivers sent the rivers above flood levels multiple times during the episode. Urban and small stream flooding also occurred.
The Chehalis River near Grand Mound and Skookumchuck River near Bucoda crested above moderate flood. Urban and small stream flooding occurred as well.
The Cowlitz River at Randle and Newaukum River near Chehalis exceeded flood stage. Urban and small stream flooding occurred also.
The Satsop River near Satsop and Chehalis River at Porter exceeded flood stage. Urban and small stream flooding also occurred.
The Skokomish River exceeded moderate flood stage. Urban and small stream flooding occurred as well.
The Snoqualmie and White Rivers exceeded flood stage. Urban and small stream flooding occurred as well. Heavy rain caused some landslides.
The Snohomish, Skykomish, and Stillaguamish Rivers exceeded flood stage. Urban and small stream flooding also occurred.  Heavy rain caused some landslides.
Heavy rain caused surface runoff, landslides, and urban and small stream flooding. One to three inches of rain fell during the day.

Heavy rain on top of saturated soils triggered a landslide that knocked a house off it's foundation, collapsing one level - destroying it and trapping the inhabitants. One man was trapped under debris and injured and had to be extricated by Seattle Fire Department. A woman was also pinned under debris but was able to escape. One dog was killed and another was found a week later in the debris and extricated. At the time, 1 to 2 inches of rain had fallen in the area in the previous 48 hours with the Seattle Antecedent Rainfall Index already high, above the threshold for heavy rain-induced landslides.

Heavy rain and snow melt on saturated soils caused a landslide in this residential neighborhood, believed to have swept away or buried a man. The slide area is the size of multiple football fields and 15 feet deep.

Heavy rain on already saturated soil cause several landslide over I-5 blocking lanes, striking vehicles, and causing collisions. Road damage occurred as well. Damages estimated for vehicles and debris removal. One injury reported.

Heavy rain on already saturated soils caused several landslides along SR 112, including a large landslide near Sekiu that cutoff the water main to the town. One section of the highway dropped 2 1/2 feet, and other locations were buried in rock, mud, and trees.
Heavy rain cause urban and small stream flooding, washing out some roads.
Strong winds caused the fairgrounds, which hosted a COVID testing, in Skagit County to be closed as of 0845am on the 15th.
Around 0200L on November 15th, strong winds caused trees to fall across Western Whatcom County, blocking all of I-5 near MP 246 for a period of time.
Strong winds caused trees to come down and block US 101 during the evening hours of November 14.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF WHATCOM AND SKAGIT COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Precipitation (snow) began during the afternoon hours on December 10, with almost 2 feet of snow measured by 8am on December 11. Snow continued through the day with another 12 plus inches by the morning of December 12. Snow gradually tapered on the 13th, with impactful snowfall finally ending by the afternoon hours.

Snow in the Olympics began during the afternoon of December 10 and quickly increased in intensity on December 11. By the time snow finally tapered during the afternoon hours of December 13, snow depth (most so observed at Hurricane Ridge) increased substantially.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF SNOHOMISH AND KING COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Snow began during the afternoon of December 10 and quickly increased in intensity, particularly over Stevens Pass, by the morning hours of December 11. In about a 24 hour period, almost 20 inches of new snow fell. Snow then continued into the 12th, with about another foot of accumulation. Snow then tapered by the afternoon hours of the 13th, with a few more inches of snow accumulations by then.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF PIERCE AND LEWIS COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Precipitation (in the form of snow) began earliest for this event in the Southern Cascades, with heavy snow already falling by the start of December 10. By the next morning (December 11), 2 feet of new snow was reported at Paradise at Mount Rainier, with the heaviest snow falling through the day on December 11. Snow continued through the 12th and into the 13th, with a fair amount of new snow accumulation before tapering by the afternoon hours of the 13th.
The ASOS at the Bellingham Airport in Western Whatcom County measured a gust of 63 mph around 1130 PM PST. A High Wind Warning was in effect for Western County County.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF PIERCE AND LEWIS COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Shortly before 11AM PST on December 11, Pierce County Sheriff noted an avalanche fatality in the Silver Basin Backcountry Ski Area on Crystal Mountain in the Southern Cascades. A total of 6 skiers were caught in the avalanche, all carrying beacons, but one person was unable to survive. High Avalanche Danger was forecast by the Northwest Avalanche Center.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF WHATCOM AND SKAGIT COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Snow began to fall around midnight on the 18th, with a quick 15 inches of new snow reported at the Mount Baker Ski Resort in a 12 hour period by noon (on the 18th). Heavy snow then continued into the 19th, with 21 inches reported in a 24 hours period at the same location previously mentioned. Snow then quickly tapered during the early morning hours of the 19th.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF SNOHOMISH AND KING COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Snow began around midnight on December 18th, with a few inches of new snow accumulation by daybreak (on the 18th). Snow then quickly became heavier, with over a foot reported in a 12 hour period from 6am on the 18th to 6pm on the 18th. Snow then quickly tapered into the 19th. Snoqualmie Pass also received new snowfall, but snowfall amounts were not heavy enough to reach winter storm criteria.

Shortly before 5 PM PST, in the heart of the evening commute, freezing rain began to fall across portions of Western Whatcom County as cold surface air from Fraser Outflow began to filter in below slightly warmer, Pacific-influenced air aloft. State troopers responded to a fatality collision involving multiple vehicles along southbound I-5 at MP 263. Roadway was fully blocked for a period of time. ||A report of around 0.05 inches of freezing rain was reported in Lynden the evening of Dec 21 with a surface temperature ranging from 28-30F.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF WHATCOM AND SKAGIT COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Heavy snow began on December 22 during the late evening hours, with 18 inches of new snow reported at the Mount Baker Ski Resort in a 24 hour period ending during the late evening hours of the 23rd. Heavy snow fell through much of the 23rd, with total snowfall pushing the 25-30 inch range by the 24th. Snow tapered for a short period of time on the 24th but quickly ramped back up on the 25th. Snow then continued through the 26th before tapering very late in the day. New snow depth reports at the Ski Resort were around 40 inches for this event.

Periods of heavy snowfall spanned across of several day period across the Olympics from Dec 22-Dec 26. Heavy snow began during the late evening hours on Dec 22nd and accumulated rapidly (according to reports from Hurricane Ridge) through Dec 23rd. Snow then finally tapered on Dec 26th.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF SNOHOMISH AND KING COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Snow began to fall in the Central Cascades during the late evening hours of Dec 22, with several inches of new snow reported at both Stevens and Snoqualmie Pass, but it wasn't until 24th when much heavier snow began. On December 24, 12 inches of new snow was received in a 12 hour period at Stevens Pass. Steady snow then continued through the 26th before then tapering off.||Although Snoqualmie Pass received a prolonged period of snowfall during these events, there was not a specific period of time where snowfall amounts met or exceeded winter storm criteria. For this prolonged event, Stevens Pass received more snowfall than Snoqualmie Pass.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF PIERCE AND LEWIS COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: A long duration period of heavy snow affected the Southern Cascades during the latter part of December. Snow began on Dec 22 and really ramped up in intensity around Dec 24-25, with about 2 feet of new snow reported after the Christmas holiday.

events.cz_name: CASCADES OF PIERCE AND LEWIS COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: A quick period of heavy snow resulted in 12-13 inches of new snow at Paradise at Mount Rainier in a 12 hour period.
Amidst strong Fraser Outflow, the ASOS at the Bellingham. Airport measured a wind gust of 63 mph around 0730 local time.

With Western Whatcom experiencing the strongest Fraser Outflow at the beginning of the winter storm event, a record low temperature was set at Bellingham of 11F, which replaces the old record of 12F set in 1971.
A record low was reported at the Quillayute ASOS on the morning of Dec 27th at 19F. This replaces the previous record low temperature of 23 from 1978.
A record low was reported at the Bellingham ASOS on the morning of Dec 27th at 9F. This replaces the previous record low temperature of 12 from 1971.
A record low was reported at the Hoquiam ASOS on the morning of Dec 27th at 25F. This replaces the previous record low temperature of 26 from 1954.
A record low was reported at the SeaTac ASOS on the morning of Dec 27th at 20F. This replaces the previous record low temperature of 22 from 1948.
A record low was reported at the SeaTac ASOS on the morning of Dec 28th at 17F. This replaces the previous record low temperature of 20F from 1968.
A record low was reported at the Hoquiam ASOS on the morning of Dec 28th at 21F. This replaces the previous record low temperature of 25F from 1978.
A winter storm brought heavy snow to Western Whatcom County around the Christmas holiday. Reports generally ranged from 8 to 15 inches.
Heavy snow affected much of Western Skagit County during the final week of December. New snow accumulations generally ranged from 6 to 12 inches.
A Winter Storm affected most of the San Juan Islands during the final week of December. Reports from the Islands generally ranged from 3 to 6 inches.

events.cz_name: EASTERN STRAIT OF JUAN DE FUCA
events.event_narrative: A Winter Storm brought heavy snow to the northern side of the Olympic Peninsula during the last week of December. Snow was orographically enhanced, resulting in an average of 10-20 inches for locations along the East Strait of Juan de Fuca, with most of the 20 inch reports located just south of Port Angeles.
A Winter Storm affected the Everett area right after the Christmas holiday as modified arctic air pushed into the area. Average snow totals ranged from 5 to 7 inches.
A Winter Storm affected the North Coast of Washington during the final week of December. Average snowfall totals were around 4 inches.

A Winter Storm affected the Central WA Coast just after the Christmas holiday. Average snowfall totals ranged generally from 3 to 6 inches, although isolated higher amounts around 9 inches were noted.
A Winter Storm brought an average of 6 to 12 inches of new snow to the Hood Canal area during the final week of December.

A Winter Storm brought heavy snow to the Southwest Interior during the last week of December as a modified arctic airmass moved in. An average of 5 to 10 inches was reported after the storm across the area.
A Winter Storm during the final week of December resulted in an average of 4 to 6 inches across the Tacoma area.
A late December Winter Storm brought an average of 3 to 5 inches to the Bremerton area as a modified arctic front pushed across the area.

A Winter Storm brought heavy snow to the Seattle area during the last week of December as a modified arctic frontal boundary pushed across the area. The Seattle metro area received an average of 4 to 6 inches of snowfall.
A Winter Storm during the last week of December resulted in an average snowfall total of 4 to 6 inches across the Bremerton area.
A winter storm brought heavy snow to the Lower Chehalis Valley Area, resulting in generally 8-12 inches of new snow accumulation.

A Winter Storm brought heavy snow to the Admiralty Inlet Area, including Whidbey Island and Camano Island. Snowfall totals in this area generally ranged from 3-8 inches, with isolated higher amounts towards 10 inches, especially the northern portion of Whidbey Island.
